'''Thomas K. Henning''' (born 9 April 1956) is a German [[astrophysicist]]. He was a director at the [[Max Planck Institute for Astronomy]] between 2001 and 2024.<ref name="mpia2024">{{Cite web |last=Jäger |first=Klaus |date=2024-05-15 |title=Myriam Benisty new director at the MPIA |url=https://www.mpia.de/6136414/2024_05_Benisty_new_Director_en |access-date=2024-05-15 |website=Max Planck Institute for Astronomy - MPIA News |language=en}}</ref> Henning is an expert in the field of [[star formation|star]] and [[planet formation]].

== Education and career ==
Henning studied physics and mathematics at the [[University of Greifswald]], specializing in [[plasma physics]]. He continued his studies at the [[University of Jena]], specializing in astronomy and astrophysics and obtaining his PhD in 1984. After joining [[Charles University in Prague]] as a postdoc (1984–1985), Henning returned to Jena where he served as an assistant at [[Jena Observatory]], completing his [[habilitation]] in 1989. After the fall of [[Berlin Wall]], he became a guest scientist at the [[Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy]] in [[Bonn]] 1989–1990 and a guest lecturer at the [[University of Cologne]] in 1991. Henning returned to the University of Jena that same year, taking over as managing scientist of the Max Planck Research Unit "Dust in Star-Forming Regions", a post he held until 1996. Henning also became a professor at Jena University in 1992.<ref name="MPG-Jena">{{Cite web |title=Scientific Member — Prof. Dr. Thomas Henning |url=https://www.mpg.de/315145/astronomy-henning |url-status=live |access-date=2026-11-06 |website=www.mpg.de |publisher=[[Max Planck Society]] |language=en}}</ref>

In 1999, Henning became Chair of Astrophysics at Jena University; a position he was to hold until 2002. At the same time, he became Director of the Astrophysical Institute and of Jena Observatory. Thomas Henning served as a guest professor at the [[University of Amsterdam]], the [[European Southern Observatory]] in [[Chile]], at [[Hokkaido University]] in [[Sapporo]], the [[University of Copenhagen]], the [[Earth–Life Science Institute]] in [[Tokyo]] as well as at [[Konkoly Observatory]] in Budapest.

Between 2000 and 2007, he was co-chair of the [[Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft|DFG]] research group "Laboratory Astrophysics" in [[Chemnitz]] and [[Jena]]. From 2001 until 2024, Henning has been a director at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, where he was head of the planetary and star formation department. After his retirement in 2024, he continued to lead a research group at MPIA and is still a scientific member. He retains his professorship at Jena and, in 2003, joined the faculty at [[Heidelberg University]] as an honorary professor.<ref name="MPG-Jena" />

== Work ==
Henning works in the field of [[star formation|star]] and [[planet formation]]. One of his areas of specialization is the observation and modelling of [[protoplanetary disks]] around young [[star]]s – an early stage in the evolution of [[planetary system]]s. To this end, Henning has also done research on the properties of interstellar [[dust]] and, more generally, on the [[physics]] and [[chemistry]] of the [[interstellar medium]] – both theoretically and using the methods of laboratory astrophysics and observational astronomy. The focus of his observational work is at [[infrared]] and [[submillimeter]] wavelengths.<ref name="Leopoldina_–_Nationale_Akademie_der_Wissenschaften-1" />

Throughout his career, Henning was and is involved in a number of major research projects, including the construction of instruments for the [[European Space Agency|ESA]] [[Herschel Space Observatory|Herschel Space Telescope]], the [[James Webb Space Telescope]] and the [[European Southern Observatory]] telescopes, the construction of the [[Large Binocular Telescope]] in [[Arizona]], the [[Spitzer Space Telescope|Spitzer]] Legacy Project "Formation of Planetary Systems", several Herschel Legacy Projects, the [[Pan-STARRS]] Survey and the [[HAT-South|HAT South]] Transit Network. He is also a fellow of the Max Planck School "Matter to Life",<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.maxplanckschools.de/17435/faculty|title=Köpfe der Max Planck School Matter to Life|website=Max Planck Schools|publisher=[[Max Planck Society]]|language=de|access-date=2019-08-22}}</ref> co-investigator of the Heidelberg [[German Universities Excellence Initiative|Excellence Cluster]] "Structures", co-investigator of the EDEN Transit Survey for the search for Earth-like planets around [[M star]]s, co-investigator of the Heidelberg-Chile [[Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite|TESS]] Exoplanet Network, head of the MPIA laboratory "Origins of Life" and founding member of the European Astrobiology Institute. In 2019, he received an ERC ([[European Research Council]]) grant of 2.5 million euros for his project "From Planet-Forming Disks to Giant Planets".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mpia.de/aktuelles/2019-04-HenningERC-E|title=Thomas Henning receives ERC Advanced Grant worth 2.5 million Euros for research of young planetary systems|date=2019-04-16|website=News & Events MPIA|publisher=MPIA|access-date=2019-08-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://erc.europa.eu/projects-figures/erc-funded-projects/results|title=ERC FUNDED PROJECTS|website=ERC: European Research Council|publisher=European Commission|language=en|access-date=2019-08-22}}</ref>

He was and is a member of a number of astronomical steering and advisory bodies, including the ESO Council, the [[Calar Alto Observatory|CAHA]] Board, the Board of Directors of LBT and PS1, and the Scientific Advisory Board of the [[Karl Schwarzschild Observatory|Thuringian State Observatory]] in [[Tautenburg]].<ref>Sections "Forschungsprojekte" and "Mitgliedschaften und Funktionen" in the entry for Thomas Henning in [http://www.uni-jena.de/suche_who_is_who.html Who's Who at the University of Jena] last accessed 2011-02-19.</ref>
